note: The machinery behind a strong SBC answer: the three parts, the ordered discourse moves inside each part, and the phrases that signal each move. Drilled in /english/rehearse/. Themes informed by a 2026 preliminary crowdsourcing resource; all scene descriptions, questions, phrasing and model answers here are original, written for this platform.
why: Every strong oral answer is built from the same small set of moves. A student who has only read model answers can recognise a good one but cannot produce one under pressure, because recognition and retrieval are different skills. This module drills retrieval.

parts.name: React to the picture
parts.job: Give a judgement and justify it from what is actually visible.
parts.examinerWants: A clear stance in the first sentence, at least one detail genuinely taken from the image, and a consequence. Hedge any guess about what a person is thinking.
parts.commonFail: Describing the picture instead of judging it. A list of what is in the frame is not an opinion.

parts.name: Tell a personal experience
parts.job: Tell one bounded incident with a turn in it, then say what it taught you.
parts.examinerWants: A specific occasion, not a habit. When, where, what happened, what changed, and a short reflection at the end.
parts.commonFail: Describing what you 'usually' or 'always' do. Habits have no turning point, so there is nothing to tell.

parts.name: Give and defend an opinion
parts.job: Take a position, support it, admit the other side, then resolve.
parts.examinerWants: A committed position, two supports with a concrete example, an honest counterpoint, and a resolution that does not sit on the fence.
parts.commonFail: Saying 'it depends' and stopping, or listing both sides without ever choosing.

moves.name: Stance
moves.job: Say what you think of it, in the first sentence, using a precise judgement word.
moves.weak: There is a girl on a bus and an old man.
moves.strong: Personally, I think the girl's action was thoughtful and considerate.
moves.whyItMatters: The examiner is listening for an opinion. A description delays it, and in a thirty second answer there is no time to recover.

moves.name: Evidence from the picture
moves.job: Point at something you can actually see, and hedge anything you are guessing.
moves.weak: He is sad because nobody helped him before.
moves.strong: From the picture, the man is leaning on a walking stick, so he might find it difficult to stand for the whole journey.
moves.whyItMatters: Anything about a person's thoughts or history is a guess. Hedging it with might or appears keeps you honest and costs nothing.

moves.name: Consequence
moves.job: Say what follows from it, for the people in the picture or for others.
moves.strong: As a result, he can travel safely, and the other passengers may be reminded to look around them too.
moves.whyItMatters: A judgement with no consequence is just a label. The consequence is what turns it into reasoning.

moves.name: Closer
moves.job: One sentence that returns to your stance so the answer sounds finished.
moves.strong: Overall, I admire her, because a small gesture like that changes the mood of a whole carriage.
moves.whyItMatters: Answers that trail off sound unprepared. A one line closer is the cheapest polish available.

moves.name: Setting
moves.job: Anchor the story to one occasion: when, where, who.
moves.weak: Sometimes I help people at the shops.
moves.strong: One Saturday morning last year, I was at the supermarket near my block with my mother.
moves.whyItMatters: One occasion can have a turning point; a habit cannot. The word sometimes is the single clearest sign an answer is about to go nowhere.

moves.name: Complication
moves.job: Introduce the problem or difficulty that makes the story worth telling.
moves.strong: I noticed an elderly woman struggling with three heavy bags while trying to pull the door open.
moves.whyItMatters: Without a difficulty there is no story, only a report. The complication is what the listener is waiting for.

moves.name: Turn
moves.job: The moment something changes, usually because of what you did.
moves.strong: She said she could manage, but I offered again, and eventually she let me carry one bag to the taxi stand.
moves.whyItMatters: A small resistance before the turn makes the story sound true. Stories where everything goes smoothly sound invented.

moves.name: Outcome
moves.strong: As a result, she reached the taxi without having to set the bags down on the wet floor.
moves.whyItMatters: The outcome is the payoff. Skipping it leaves the examiner waiting for an ending that never comes.

moves.name: Reflection
moves.job: One sentence on what it taught you or changed in you.
moves.strong: Since then I have paid much more attention to people who are carrying too much, because I had walked past that same door many times without noticing anyone.
moves.whyItMatters: This is the sentence that separates a child telling a story from a candidate answering a question. It is also the easiest mark to forget.

moves.name: Position
moves.job: Commit to a side in the first sentence. A partial position is fine, but it must be a position.
moves.strong: In my opinion, most people here do behave considerately, although there is still room for improvement.
moves.whyItMatters: It depends, on its own, answers nothing. Adding although there is still room for improvement turns a fence-sit into a real position.

moves.name: Support
moves.job: Give the reason your position holds.
moves.strong: This is because most commuters have grown up with constant reminders, so giving up a seat has become close to automatic.
moves.whyItMatters: Firstly is worth saying out loud even if you only have one reason. It tells the examiner your answer has a structure.

moves.name: Example
moves.job: One concrete instance. Named, specific, short.
moves.strong: For instance, I have often seen passengers move down the carriage without being asked so that more people can board.
moves.whyItMatters: An abstract argument sounds rehearsed. One specific example makes the whole answer sound like it came from a real life.

moves.name: Counterpoint
moves.job: Admit the honest weakness in your own position.
moves.strong: However, not everyone is so aware. Some commuters become so engrossed in their phones that they do not notice a person standing right beside them.
moves.whyItMatters: Conceding the other side makes you sound fair rather than weak, and it is where the more advanced vocabulary usually lands.

moves.name: Resolution
moves.job: Come back and settle it. Do not leave both sides standing.
moves.weak: So both sides have a point.
moves.strong: Overall, I believe most people here behave well, but the gap is attention rather than kindness, and that is something reminders can fix.
moves.whyItMatters: The counterpoint opens a door; the resolution has to close it. An answer that ends on the counterpoint sounds like you changed your mind.

scenes.title: Giving up a seat on the bus
scenes.scene: A crowded single-deck bus in the late afternoon. A girl in school uniform, backpack still on her shoulders, has stood up from the priority seat and stepped back into the aisle. An elderly man with a walking stick is lowering himself carefully into the seat she has left. Two other passengers nearby are looking at their phones. Through the window, the sky has started to darken.

questions.stem: What do you think of the girl's action? Why?
Tell me about a time when you helped someone who needed it, or saw someone else do so.
Do you think people in Singapore behave considerately on public transport? Why or why not?

scenes.title: A beach clean-up
scenes.scene: A stretch of sand on an overcast morning. Six students in matching yellow vests are spread across the beach, each holding a bag. One is crouching to pick up a tangle of fishing line; another has stopped to look at a plastic bottle half buried in the sand. A full bag already stands upright near the tideline. Further out, a container ship sits on the horizon.

questions.stem: Why do you think these students are taking part in this activity?
Tell me about a time you took part in something that helped the environment or your community. How did you feel?
How much difference can children really make to protecting the environment?

scenes.title: A phone at the dinner table
scenes.scene: A family of four at dinner in a small flat. The mother is mid-sentence, turned towards the father, who is laughing. A younger sister is reaching across for a dish. The boy at the end of the table has his head down, both thumbs on his phone, and his rice is untouched. The television behind them is off.

questions.stem: What do you think of the boy's behaviour during dinner? Why?
Tell me about a time you played a game with your family, on a screen or on a board. Which did you enjoy more, and why?
Do you think children today spend too much time on digital devices? Why or why not?

scenes.title: Loud phones on the train
scenes.scene: A train carriage in the evening. Two boys share one phone between them, held up so both can see, and both are laughing loudly with their heads tipped back. A woman opposite has closed her eyes and turned her face away. An older man beside her glances up from his newspaper. Nobody has said anything.

questions.stem: What is your opinion of the boys' behaviour on the train?
Tell me about a time someone's behaviour disturbed you in a public place. What happened?
How can people use their devices in public without disturbing those around them?
